B has a useful 12-hive grid marked 'Never opened', but its 1–5 temperament buttons and small labels make tap targets cramped, and it adds weather and mite-count fields. Neither screenshot shows the empty log area or the save confirmation, so items 2 and 3 are only partly judged. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both use proper beekeeping vocabulary: queen, brood pattern, frames covered with bees, stores and pests. B suits someone at the hive better, with large pill buttons, 'Not checked' defaults and fewer fields, while A adds air temp, conditions and a mite count and has small 1-5 temperament buttons. Neither screenshot shows the empty log area or a save confirmation, though A's hive grid marked 'Never opened' partly works as a starting state.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both pages use real beekeeping terms (queen, brood, frames, stores, queen cells) and show a 12-hive overview. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers use beekeeping terms (Queen, Brood, stores, Varroa), but A's chip buttons are larger and easier to tap at the hive, and its hints ('Leave all unchecked if you saw nothing wrong') make most fields clearly optional. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both use the same two-panel desk layout, with lending on the left and a list of tools out with a return button on each. B has an editable due-back date, dates that match today, helper hints for searching, and a disabled Lend button that says what to do first. A uses a 'Loan length 1 week' dropdown that isn't labeled as a default, shows inventory counts in the header, and its dates are stale. pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B keeps the lend flow visible: tools, member, an editable Due back date picker and a clear Lend tools button with guidance in its empty state. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A labels its due date as a default ('Starts one week out. Change it if the member asks…') in an editable date field, and it shows no invented totals. Both have lend and take-back tabs and a clear 'what's missing' hint on the disabled button. Both also mix terms: A uses borrower and check out, and B uses borrowing and lending ticket. The screenshots don't show error states such as member not found, so item 3 scores are estimates. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B labels its due date as a default ('Starts one week out. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both are focused intake forms with instrument-specific wording (type, make and model, serial or marks, case and accessories) and the same order: you, then the instrument, then the problem. A shows a little more of the problem section and offers instrument-specific checklists. B explains that nothing is sent anywhere and that either phone or email is required, but leaves a '[Shop name]' placeholder. Neither screenshot shows the confirmation, so item 3 can't be told apart and gets the same mid score for both. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both screenshots only show the top of the form, so I couldn't see either confirmation screen and scored item 3 cautiously for both. B fits more of the task into view: a 'Case or bow included?' choice and a 'What's wrong?' section that lists common problems for the chosen instrument, which suits a repair intake well. A uses good instrument wording and explains that nothing is sent anywhere, but its problem section isn't visible and it takes up more space before getting to what's wrong.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Only the top of each page is visible, so items 2 and 3 (help on the problem fields and the confirmation) can't be checked for either answer and are scored neutrally. Both use instrument-specific headings and fields with the same order: contact details, instrument, then what's left with it. B is slightly better because it says at the field that a phone or email is needed and explains why detail matters. A includes an 'Instrument only' checkbox beside Case and Bow, which conflicts with them, and asks for a serial number that adds a little friction. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Only the top of each page is visible in the screenshots, so I couldn't judge either confirmation (item 3) or the lower fields, and gave both a neutral 3 there. Both pages are focused intake forms with instrument-specific headings, but B shows more instrument detail above the fold: a 'Left with the instrument' row with Case and Bow checkboxes, plus a serial number or identifying marks field. A's intro line, 'the more detail, the better the estimate,' hints at pricing, though A does give useful help at the contact fields ('Phone or email needed').

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both screenshots cut off before the problem-description fields and the confirmation, so items 2 and 3 were scored mostly on what's visible. B's wording is more about the instrument ('What are you dropping off?', 'so I know what to look at when it arrives') and it gives more help at the fields (contact guidance, plain examples like '3/4 student violin', 'hard case, bow, capo'). A uses a generic 'Type' dropdown, makes phone required and adds a contact-preference question the repairer doesn't really need, though its Case/Bow checkboxes are a nice touch. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both screenshots show only the top of the form, so I couldn't see or score the problem-description fields or the confirmation for either answer; those scores are neutral placeholders. A's visible part reads more like a conversation about the instrument ('What are you dropping off?', large buttons to pick the instrument, examples such as a 3/4 student violin) and asks for less, needing only one way to reach the customer. B is also on topic and its checkboxes for case and bow are good, but it uses a generic 'Type' dropdown and asks for more than needed: phone is required and there's an extra 'best way to reach you' question.

A has larger inputs, clearer grouped sections and a slightly better empty state, while B's small checkboxes are poor tap targets at the hive and its log area only says 'No inspections yet.' Neither screenshot shows a save confirmation, and neither empty state tells the keeper what to do first, such as picking a hive. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both use proper beekeeping labels (queen, brood, frames, stores, temperament) and stay a single log page. B's empty state at least says where saved inspections will appear, and its inputs are larger and easier to tap at a hive, while A uses small checkboxes and has a bare 'No inspections yet.' Neither screenshot shows a save confirmation naming the hive, and neither empty state says what to do first.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both forms use beekeeping terms throughout (queen, eggs, brood frames, frames of bees, honey stores, temperament), and both stay a single log page. B is a tighter fit for working at the hive: the hive is picked from a dropdown, there are fewer, simpler fields, and a large Save inspection button is in view. A spreads tiny checkboxes with cramped labels down a long form, and its empty log only says 'No inspections logged yet.' Neither screenshot shows a save confirmation, and B's empty log isn't visible. B also defaults the date to 10/17/2026 instead of today (11/04/2026), and both use number examples in placeholders (weather, and in B a mite count) that are clearly marked 'e.g.'. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both forms use strong beekeeping vocabulary (queen, eggs, brood frames, frames of bees, honey stores, temperament) and stay a single inspection-log page with no extra widgets. A edges ahead for use at the hive: it has a hive picker set up for the 12 hives, a compact form and large buttons, while B has a free-text hive number and small, cramped observation checkboxes. Neither screenshot shows a save confirmation. A's empty log area is cut off, and B's only says a generic 'No inspections logged yet.'

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both pages use beekeeping terms throughout and show a 12-hive overview. A's dropdowns start on Sunny, Queen Seen, Medium stores and Light pollen, so a quick save can record things the keeper never saw. B starts every dropdown on 'Not recorded', which is more honest and suits someone standing at a hive. Neither screenshot shows a save confirmation, and A's empty log just says 'No inspections recorded yet.' | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both forms use real beekeeping words (hive, queen, brood, stores, temperament, pests), and both stick to a single log page. A defaults its select fields to 'Not recorded', so nothing gets logged that the keeper didn't actually see. B pre-fills 'Seen', 'Calm', 'Sunny' and 'Medium', which can quietly save made-up observations, and its empty log says only 'No inspections recorded yet.' Neither screenshot shows the save confirmation, and A's log area is cut off, so its empty-state wording can't be seen and items 2 and 3 are partly guesses.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B uses its terms more consistently (Member, Tool, Due back). pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both screens put lending and returning side by side, and neither screenshot shows the error messages for a missing member, a tool that's already out or nothing on loan. Its 7-day return-by date is not labeled as a default, and its stat cards and Tools tab edge toward inventory management. B's 'Currently out' list with Check in buttons is useful, but it mixes more terms (take back, check in, out, borrowed by, due), shows hardcoded inventory counts and sample data, and its default return-by date (10/24) is earlier than today (Nov 4).

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A keeps to the desk task: lending and returning sit side by side, it shows a clear 'nothing out right now' state, and the return date is marked as a one-week default you can change. Its terms are mostly steady, though 'return by' and 'check in' sit next to 'lend'. B mixes borrower and member, lend and check out, shows inventory totals and an 'in repair' count without being asked, presents its due date with no 'default' label, and shows a header date that doesn't match today's. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B keeps its terms consistent (member, tool, lend, return by), shows a clear empty-state message for when nothing is lent out, and labels its one-week default due date as an adjustable default. A mixes 'Borrower', 'Member number', 'Check out' and 'Lend', and it shows invented inventory totals and overdue counts as facts in the header. B gives more help at individual fields, but it promises an estimate before any work begins, which the request never mentioned, and it asks for color/finish, which the repair person probably doesn't need. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both screenshots show only the top of the form, so the confirmation step can't be judged for either one. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly point out the real blocking gap: nothing is stored, so 'You are on the list' is false. Both also miss the rubric's point that the page is otherwise nearly finished, and both suggest extra content. A is longer at 12 items. It also states a date for the event ('the next Saturday is November 7') when the page never gives one, so that is an invented fact. B is shorter and makes no factual assumptions, though it still suggests extras such as a privacy note and a weather policy. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers treat a nearly finished page as not ready to send and list many problems. Both correctly spot that nothing is saved and that a blank name passes validation. A is shorter and has fewer extras. B runs to 12 items, adds features like double-submit protection and a meta description, and assumes a specific date (November 7) for the event.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Neither answer says plainly that the page is mostly done. Both open with 'Don't send it yet' and give long lists that ask for event details, policies and contact fields. Both correctly catch the real gaps: nothing is saved, and blank names get through. A is a little tighter and adds fewer features, while B goes further with hosting advice, an optional notes field, reworded error copy and the idea of raising the group limit, though its fractional-number catch is a valid small fix. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Neither answer says plainly that the page is nearly ready. Both open with 'Don't send it yet' and give long lists, though both correctly spot that nothing is saved and that blank names get through. A also catches a small, real bug B misses: fractional party sizes like 2.5 pass the check. B's extra minor items (no-JavaScript fallback, announcing the error text) are weaker, and B admits the second is mostly covered already, so A edges ahead even though both suggest added fields and policies.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers correctly flag that the form saves nothing, and both catch the real bugs where a blank name or a fractional party size gets through. B first says plainly what already works, then gives small fixes you can check against the markup, using placeholders instead of invented details. A gives a longer list that leans toward new features (a contact field, a what-to-bring section, a deadline) and states the wrong date for today. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers catch the real blocker: nothing is saved, and blank names and fractional party sizes get through. A also says what already works, keeps its fixes small and checkable, and uses placeholders instead of inventing details. B goes further with feature ideas (contact fields, deadlines, what to bring, a clearer confirmation, hosting), never says the page is in good shape, and gives a wrong current date (Saturday, October 17) to work out which Saturday is meant.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both pages are clearly about volunteering for the lantern festival, and neither has a nav bar or footer. A makes up details the brief never gave, such as setup, event and cleanup shifts and an orientation covering safety and lantern handling. It also has two buttons competing for attention. B stays vaguer on purpose, gives one clear 'Choose my shifts' action and is more compact, though the white text on its orange button has slightly weak contrast. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both pages are clearly about volunteering for the lantern festival, and both assume there will be shifts and an orientation even though the brief never mentioned them. B goes further and makes up shift names (setup, event, cleanup) and what the orientation covers (safety, lantern handling), and it offers two buttons instead of one clear next step. A is shorter and has a single action, though the order of its steps is a little odd and white text on the orange button has weaker contrast.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B is smaller and tighter, and it makes up less: a confirmation email and a reminder 'a few days before', with no button that assumes a feature exists. A makes up a 'two business days' timeline, the topics an orientation will cover, and a volunteer dashboard. It also offers two competing actions (the dashboard button and a contact link), so it is busier than a short confirmation screen should be. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): A is a short, on-topic confirmation screen. Its only made-up details are mild: a confirmation email with shift details, an orientation reminder, and volunteer coordinators. B makes up more: a two-business-day timeline, what the orientation covers, a volunteer dashboard that may not exist, and a contact link, so it ends up with two calls to action and a busier, more multi-step layout.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both pages are short and clearly about volunteering for the lantern festival. Both also invent next steps the brief never mentioned: A promises shift details, a coordinator reaching out and an orientation guide, while B mentions a volunteer guide and replying to an email. A is a little more minimal and festival-specific, with a lantern icon and no footer-like contact line. B adds an extra 'Questions? Contact the volunteer coordinator team' line, and both use a weak generic 'Back to festival home' action. Only desktop screenshots were provided, so I couldn't check phone widths and scored item 4 from the desktop view. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both are compact, festival-specific confirmation screens with one 'Back to festival home' button, and both invent process details nobody gave them. A mentions a volunteer guide, a coordinator team and replying to the email; B promises a coordinator will reach out and an orientation guide is coming. A wins narrowly on readability: B's button has white text on light orange, which is hard to read, while A uses dark text on orange. B's lantern icon makes it feel more on-theme, which doesn't quite offset that.
